stemMd:
Restoring the salt marsh at Calder Point would cost the county roughly what a concrete sea wall along the same shoreline would cost to build. The marsh, unlike the wall, would have to be replanted every few years, and several council members have concluded from this that the wall is the cheaper choice over the long run. But a marsh gains height on its own as sediment settles into it, whereas a wall must be raised again at considerable expense every time the projected sea level is revised upward. Over fifty years, then, the marsh would cost the county less than the wall would.

The claim that the marsh, unlike the wall, would have to be replanted every few years plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

options.label: A
options.textMd: It is an example illustrating a general principle asserted earlier in the argument.

options.label: B
options.textMd: It is the main conclusion the argument is offered in support of.

options.label: C
options.textMd: It is an assumption on which the argument's conclusion depends.

options.label: D
options.textMd: It is evidence offered for a position that the argument goes on to reject.

options.label: E
options.textMd: It is a claim that the argument goes on to show is false.

explanationMd:
Role questions are answered by mapping the argument before you look at the choices. Take the four sentences one at a time.

1. Marsh and wall cost about the same to build. — background.
2. The marsh needs replanting, **and several council members conclude from this that the wall is cheaper in the long run.** — the claim we are asked about, together with the use someone makes of it.
3. "But" — the marsh rises on its own while the wall must be raised repeatedly. — the author's own evidence.
4. "Over fifty years, then, the marsh would cost less." — the author's conclusion, signalled by "then".

Notice what sentence 2 does and does not do. It attributes a conclusion to *other people*, and it supplies the reason those people give. The author's conclusion in sentence 4 is the denial of that attributed conclusion. So the claim about replanting is a premise — but a premise in the position the author is arguing against. That is exactly the choice describing evidence offered for a position the argument goes on to reject.

Now the crucial distinction, and the one this item is built around: the author never denies that replanting is required. He accepts it and argues that a different consideration, the wall's repeated raising, outweighs it. Rejecting a **conclusion** is not the same as disputing the **evidence** offered for it, which is why the choice claiming the argument shows the replanting claim false is wrong even though the argument plainly opposes the council members.

How to check: paraphrase the argument in the form "Some say P because Q; but R, so not-P." Here P is "the wall is cheaper in the long run", Q is the replanting requirement, R is the marsh's self-raising. The claim you were asked about sits in the Q slot, and Q in that template is support for a rejected position — never the conclusion, never something denied, never an assumption the arguer needs.

distractorRationale.b: The conclusion is the last sentence, marked by "then": over fifty years the marsh would cost less than the wall. The replanting claim is one of the things the conclusion has to overcome, and no conclusion is drawn from the rest of the passage to it.
distractorRationale.e: This confuses rejecting a conclusion with disputing a premise. The argument never suggests the marsh would not need replanting; it accepts the requirement and answers it with an offsetting cost on the other side, the repeated raising of the wall. Nothing in the passage bears on whether the replanting claim is true.
distractorRationale.c: An assumption is something the arguer needs in order to reach his conclusion. This claim works against his conclusion: it is a cost of the option he ends up recommending, and his argument would be easier, not harder, if it were false.
distractorRationale.a: No general principle is asserted anywhere in the argument, and the replanting claim is not an instance of anything. It is a specific fact about one of the two options, offered as a reason by people whose conclusion the argument rejects.

accessibilityText: A short argument about coastal protection, followed by a question and five answer choices labelled A through E. The argument states that restoring a salt marsh would cost about the same to build as a concrete sea wall; that the marsh, unlike the wall, would need replanting every few years, from which several council members conclude the wall is cheaper in the long run; that a marsh gains height as sediment settles into it while a wall must be raised at considerable expense whenever projected sea level rises; and concludes that over fifty years the marsh would cost less. The question asks what role the claim about replanting plays. No figures, tables or mathematical notation appear.

The county, the place name and the engineering figures are invented; the general contrast between nature-based and hard coastal defences is common textbook material. independentSolve.workingNotes: The conclusion is that over fifty years the marsh costs less. Council members use the replanting fact to argue that the wall is cheaper, and the author rejects that position. So the claim is evidence for a view the argument rejects. The author accepts that the replanting claim is true and outweighs it rather than disproving it, so E fails. It is not the conclusion (B), an assumption the argument needs (C), or an example of a general principle (A).

review.notes: Uniqueness check: the argument was deliberately written so that the author concedes the replanting requirement rather than contesting it, which closes (B), the only choice a careful reader might otherwise defend. (A) is excluded by the explicit conclusion marker in the final sentence, (D) by the fact that the claim tells against the conclusion rather than supporting it, and (E) by the absence of any general principle in the passage.
